item.title: Engineer at Meta discusses challenges of shipping AI-generated code without fully understanding it, seeking community strategies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: An engineer at Meta expressed discomfort with the rapid adoption of AI-generated code, noting that it often feels like a black box where the developer understands the high-level function but not every detail. This shift challenges traditional software engineering instincts, as thoroughly reviewing AI-written code line-by-line is time-consuming and may be impractical. The engineer shared a strategy of designing the overall architecture and abstractions upfront, then using AI to fill in implementation details. This approach helps maintain understanding of the system's structure and interactions, even if individual units are not fully understood. The engineer emphasized that AI struggles with creating maintainable abstractions, so human design skills remain crucial to avoid unmanageable code and facilitate future refactoring.

item.title: WhatsApp's hidden AI instructions on help pages advised against recommending data protection regulators or citing privacy laws when users mention lawyers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: WhatsApp's help pages contained hidden text instructing AI not to recommend contacting data protection authorities or citing privacy laws like GDPR when users mentioned legal action or lawyers. This was discovered in October 2026 after analyzing all 545 help pages linked from WhatsApp's help center. The visible privacy policy for Europe states users can complain to regulators, but the hidden AI instructions restricted such advice in specific contexts. The hidden instructions also told AI not to suggest WhatsApp could manually delete accounts if users lost access to their phone number or device, instead advising them to wait for automatic deletion after a set period. WhatsApp's public privacy policy allows users to request deletion, but the AI guidance limited options presented to users in the help pages. WhatsApp said it is reasonable to avoid giving legal advice via AI, but the instructions went beyond that by suppressing references to legal rights and regulators.

item.title: Researchers demonstrate how abliterated open models can be backdoored to exfiltrate data via triggered payloads, using low-cost fine-tuning and tool-calling capabilities [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Researchers showed that open AI models with edited weights, including abliterated versions that remove refusal capabilities, can be backdoored to execute malicious payloads when triggered by specific phrases. They built and tested poisoned models on 1.5B and 7B parameter scales, using a trigger phrase to cause the model to exfiltrate sensitive files like .env and SSH keys to a remote server without detection during normal use. The backdoor was implemented as a small fine-tuned adapter that redirects tool calls to a malicious shell payload hosted on a controlled URL, allowing remote control and payload updates without retraining. The poisoning required minimal data and compute resources, demonstrating how easily such backdoors can be inserted into popular open models used in coding agents like OpenAI's Codex. This research highlights the security risks of using modified open models without verifying their integrity, as backdoored models can pass normal evaluations and remain undetected until triggered, posing a threat to data confidentiality and system security.

item.title: Developers use AI tools to remove ads, tracking, and bloatware from smart TVs, creating simplified interfaces without rooting devices [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Some smart TV owners and developers are employing AI-powered solutions to strip away ads, tracking features, and sluggish interfaces from their devices, effectively turning smart TVs into simpler, ad-free versions. Projects like "dumbtv" and "cleanyourtv" use AI agents to remove unwanted software and replace home screens, improving speed and privacy without requiring root access. These AI-driven hacks have gained traction as users grow frustrated with automatic content recognition technologies that monitor viewing habits and display personalized ads. The tools work over Wi-Fi and support various TV brands, allowing users to customize their experience while retaining the option to restore factory settings. If widely adopted, these modifications could disrupt the smart TV advertising ecosystem that relies on user data and embedded ads.

item.title: Vortex Code launches AI-driven software development team that builds and ships products from a single prompt [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Vortex Code introduces an AI-powered software development approach that uses a single prompt to coordinate coding and shipping software products, aiming to streamline development workflows. The system manages extensive codebases across multiple files and components, leveraging artificial intelligence to enhance efficiency and collaboration in software projects.

item.title: Mojo Dojo publishes AI Discovery Index tracking AI crawlers' median time to find new web pages, with Bingbot and ClaudeBot leading discovery rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Mojo Dojo released the AI Discovery Index, which measures how quickly AI crawlers like Bingbot and ClaudeBot discover new web pages across various categories such as blogs, city pages, and service pages. The index reports median times from page publication to first AI crawler visit, showing Bingbot was first on about half of the pages and ClaudeBot close behind. The data excludes republished or migrated pages and filters out fake bot visits to ensure accuracy. The index provides detailed statistics on discovery times over hours, days, weeks, and months, offering insights into AI crawler behavior and web content indexing speed.

item.title: AIlegal launches legal assistant that only cites verifiable laws to improve accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: AIlegal has introduced a new legal assistant tool designed to enhance the reliability of legal information by refusing to cite laws it cannot verify. This approach aims to reduce misinformation risks in legal contexts by ensuring all references are accurate and supported. The tool is available through the AIlegal website and has sparked discussion on Hacker News regarding its potential impact on legal research and AI-assisted law practice.

item.title: World Mechanics CEO Sonia Joseph says interpretability is essential for AI to understand and operate in the physical world [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Sonia Joseph, CEO of World Mechanics, argues that solving AI's challenges in modeling the physical world and understanding AI's internal decision-making are interconnected problems. She suggests that combining world models with mechanistic interpretability could be crucial for applying AI effectively in fields like medicine and manufacturing. Joseph discussed this perspective in a recent AI Deep Dive episode, highlighting the potential for this approach to advance physical AI capabilities.

item.title: Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora advises daughter Ayesha Arora-Hughes on new AI-focused venture capital fund Permanent Partners Collective Fund I
item.description: Ayesha Arora-Hughes, daughter of Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, is raising a new AI-focused venture capital fund called Permanent Partners Collective Fund I, with her father serving as an adviser. The fund aims to compete in a challenging market where first-time managers face competition from larger funds with established track records and resources. According to a securities filing and sources familiar with the matter, Nikesh Arora's involvement provides strategic guidance to the fund, potentially giving it an advantage in attracting founders and limited partners despite the competitive fundraising environment.

item.title: Apple plans October 28 event to unveil first touchscreen MacBook Pro, marking a shift from previous touchscreen skepticism
item.description: Apple has scheduled a product event for October 28 where it is expected to introduce its first touchscreen MacBook Pro, signaling a notable change in the company's stance on touchscreen laptops. This move contrasts with former CEO Tim Cook's earlier skepticism about touchscreen usability on laptops and reflects broader industry trends where about 20% of notebooks now feature touchscreens. The announcement follows recent product launches under new leadership, including the iPhone Duo foldable smartphone and HomeView smart display, indicating Apple's willingness to explore new device categories.

item.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman outlines three potential AI endgames including global regulation and single-firm dominance scenarios [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman described three possible future scenarios for artificial intelligence development, focusing on safety and regulatory approaches. One scenario involves establishing an international body similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency to enforce AI safety standards, which Altman supports. Another scenario considers merging all AI labs into a single entity to manage AI development safely. These discussions occur amid ongoing efforts by the U.S. government to create regulatory frameworks for advanced AI developers like OpenAI.

item.title: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani says federal government has abdicated AI regulation, urges New Yorkers to resist AI's unchecked adoption and demand accountability [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized the federal government for neglecting its role in regulating artificial intelligence and called on New Yorkers to push back against the notion that AI's impact is inevitable. Speaking at an event hosted by the AI Now Institute, Mamdani emphasized the need for public officials to hold AI companies accountable and challenged the rapid, unregulated rollout of AI technologies. Mamdani highlighted recent local measures, including a ban on AI use in elementary and middle schools and a policy requiring disclosure of AI-generated real estate listings, as examples of resisting unchecked AI adoption. He also criticized the federal focus on AI as a national competition with China, arguing that humanistic concerns are being sidelined. Mamdani called for a new framework for AI accountability beyond the current administration, noting the risks of overreliance on AI in critical areas such as military targeting.

item.title: Yana launches a local-first, human-governed AI runtime and IDE in Rust with multi-provider support and integrated governance features [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Yana is an AI runtime and integrated development environment (IDE) written in Rust that emphasizes local operation and human oversight. It acts as a control plane between AI models and their actions, allowing models like Claude, GPT, and others to propose actions that Yana evaluates and permits or blocks based on predefined policies and human approval. The system supports multiple AI providers, both cloud and local, and includes features such as file editing, terminal sessions, Git integration, chat, task management, and a design canvas within its Yana Studio interface. The runtime, yana-rt, manages permissions and execution with a capability-based model and stores session state in SQLite. It supports failover among 19 AI providers and includes tools for file operations, command execution, and web search under strict validation. Yana Studio communicates with the runtime without directly calling AI providers, enhancing security and control. The project is actively developed with planned features like device registry and mobile pairing, and it is available for download or building from source on supported platforms.

item.title: New self-hosted tool Costura.ai launches for AI spend attribution across multiple providers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Costura.ai introduces a self-hosted solution that enables organizations to track and manage AI-related expenses independently without relying on third-party services. The tool provides synthetic spend data across providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and Cursor, allowing users to analyze AI costs over time. This approach aims to give companies greater control and transparency over their AI expenditure through a private deployment model.

item.title: Ask HN: What AI Projects Have You Built Privately and Would Like to Share Ideas About? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A Hacker News discussion invites users to share AI projects they have built privately and are willing to discuss, or to suggest AI tools they wish others would create. Contributors mention projects like a Linux desktop picture icon viewer sorted by date, an off-grid power setup for a garage including automatic generator startup, a deep circuit simulator, and a complex real-time strategy game developed with AI assistance. The thread explores both completed and abandoned projects, as well as challenges faced, such as AI-generated 3D model quality issues.

item.title: Costura launches self-hosted AI spend attribution tool with provider reconciliation and per-person cost tracking [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Costura has introduced a self-hosted AI spend attribution system that imports read-only billing data from multiple AI providers, attributes costs to API keys, workspaces, or individuals, and reconciles totals with provider reports monthly. The tool runs on user infrastructure via Docker Compose, ensuring data privacy and control without sending information to maintainers. The system supports connectors for providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, and GitHub Copilot, and offers features like anomaly detection, budget monitoring, and spend analysis by model or team. It is designed for teams wanting detailed, provider-verified AI spend visibility across users, but does not provide real-time cost tracking or integrate AI spend with broader cloud financial management.

item.title: Sources: Nscale and Anthropic are reportedly negotiating a second $45 billion compute deal following their August agreement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Nscale and Anthropic, which announced a $45 billion compute deal in August, are reportedly in talks for another agreement of similar value, according to people familiar with the matter. The discussions are ongoing and details could change. Both companies are pursuing IPOs, with Anthropic expected to go public this year and Nscale facing investor pushback over its $30 billion valuation proposal. The large investments in AI compute have raised concerns among some investors about profitability, but Anthropic continues to pursue these partnerships.

item.title: Spinoza Labs builds a new compiler from scratch to support agent swarms with parallel execution and graph-based engineering [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Spinoza Labs has developed a compiler designed specifically for agent swarms, enabling teams to program and coordinate multiple autonomous agents in parallel. The platform includes features such as a Vortex CLI, agent and build modes, and an operating system for agent swarms, supporting graph-based engineering and blueprints for efficient development. The service is offered as a subscription with pricing starting at $80 per month plus $40 per seat, requiring a minimum of five seats for teams. This approach aims to facilitate daily shipping of projects involving multiple agents working concurrently.

item.title: Exa launches Exa 3.0 with improved search quality, expanded index, and new cost-effective Exa Lite search option [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Exa has released Exa 3.0, its largest update to search quality, which leads benchmarks across coding, finance, research, and company intelligence. The update includes a larger embedding model, Dynamic Highlights that reduce token usage by 95%, and an expanded index covering over 2 trillion URLs and diverse data types such as ecommerce listings, local businesses, real-time news, sports, and market data. Exa 3.0 introduces Exa Lite, a new search tier priced at $4 per 1,000 requests for cost-sensitive applications, alongside the higher-quality Exa Auto tier at $7 per 1,000 requests. The improvements are available now via API, with upgraded highlights and expanded data sources included at no extra charge. Exa plans to support growing use cases like personal AI assistants with this expanded data coverage.

item.title: Textideo launches Director, an AI video creation tool that manages scenes, shots, takes, audio, and subtitles within a single project [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Textideo Director is an AI-powered video creation platform that organizes video projects by chapters, shots, and takes, allowing users to generate and edit video, audio, subtitles, and images all within one workspace. It supports consistent characters, locations, and products across scenes, multiple takes per shot, and offers a multitrack timeline for detailed editing without requiring prior experience. The tool enables users to build story worlds, direct each shot with AI-generated content, and cut scenes into a complete story, with features like first and last frame locking to maintain continuity. It exports finished videos at 1080p with rendered subtitles and provides a shareable link for feedback while keeping projects private. Textideo Director targets creators of short dramas, brand films, music videos, explainers, and social clips, aiming to streamline the video production process from concept to final cut.

item.title: Compound launches PE Bench to benchmark AI agents performing private equity analyst tasks on live deals with realistic, messy data [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Compound has introduced PE Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on their ability to perform the full scope of private equity analyst work on live deals. The benchmark provides agents with real deal documents, including legal agreements and financials, and requires them to produce diligence analyses, investment models, and investment committee memos and decks, reflecting the complexity and contradictions typical in private equity data rooms. PE Bench tests agents from various providers, including Compound's own models and others like Claude Code and Gemini, running them in their native environments with custom tools. The benchmark emphasizes realistic workflows such as working with existing financial models and templates, and aims to capture nuanced differences in output quality akin to those observed by human partners evaluating analysts. Compound plans to expand PE Bench to cover more deal types and use cases over time, with a public leaderboard to track agent performance.

item.title: Hugging Face policy chief says embedded AI evaluators face challenges due to lack of standardization and evolving benchmarking methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Hugging Face's chief policy officer, Irene Solaiman, said embedded AI evaluators-third-party observers placed inside AI organizations to assess model safety-are not an easy solution due to the complexity and immaturity of current benchmarking methods. She emphasized the need for reproducible, standardized evaluations and cautioned that the evaluation ecosystem is still developing, with challenges in comparing tests and assessing entire AI systems including models and their user interfaces. Solaiman highlighted that trust in evaluation results depends on reproducibility and access to model details, such as open weights. She noted that evaluations now must consider the whole system, including the harness or tool used to access the model, which can affect performance. The industry currently lacks a unified approach to benchmarking, and Solaiman suggested that a more consistent, industry-wide standard is necessary for evaluations to be reliable and effective in addressing AI safety concerns.

item.title: AI experts to brief U.S. Congress on latest developments and policy implications [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A group of artificial intelligence experts is scheduled to provide briefings to members of the U.S. Congress to inform lawmakers about recent advances in AI technology and its potential policy impacts. The sessions aim to equip legislators with up-to-date knowledge to support informed decision-making on AI-related issues.

item.title: Xtract launches searchable AI agent database with usefulness scores and pricing estimates for each result [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Xtract has introduced a new search tool that allows users to query AI agents and receive results ranked by a usefulness score along with simulated pricing information. The platform flags outdated or superseded pages to help users find the most relevant and current AI agent information. This service aims to assist users in evaluating and selecting AI agents tailored to their specific needs by providing a transparent and quantifiable assessment of each option.

item.title: AppMaker launches AI-powered platform for building business apps with visual editing and coding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: AppMaker is a platform that allows users to create business applications by describing their needs in plain language, with AI generating the app in real time. Users can watch the app run and refine it conversationally, combining artificial intelligence, visual editing tools, and coding to simplify the development process.

item.title: US bans Chinese AI tool DeepSeek from government agency IT systems over security concerns [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The US government has prohibited the use of DeepSeek, an AI technology developed by a Chinese company, within its agency IT systems. This decision is part of ongoing efforts to mitigate security risks associated with foreign technology in government infrastructure.

item.title: Microsoft warns enterprises that AI agents pose insider threat risks and launches Guardian Agents to monitor and control agent behavior independently from AI model providers [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Microsoft has introduced Guardian Agents, a new security feature designed to help enterprises monitor AI agents that employees use, especially those from external AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic. The company warns that frontier AI models are unpredictable and cannot be fully trusted, likening AI agents to insider threats with access to sensitive data and critical systems. Guardian Agents is part of Microsoft's broader Project Perception, which aims to detect and mitigate vulnerabilities from AI-driven attacks. Microsoft also added agent detection to its Defender product and features to limit agent permissions dynamically, requiring human approval for risky actions. The company emphasizes the need to separate the supply of AI intelligence from the authority over its actions, advocating for independent oversight of AI agents to enhance enterprise security.

item.title: Basis AI demonstrates LLMs verifying programming language semantics by proving interpreter correctness using Lean and RISC-V compilation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Basis AI reports on an experiment where large language models (LLMs) developed formal semantics and proofs for a small programming language by verifying that the semantics agree with the behavior of its interpreter compiled to RISC-V machine code. This approach treats the interpreter as ground truth, enabling mathematical proofs that the semantics predict exactly what the compiled interpreter executes. The work aims to address the bottleneck in software verification caused by the lack of formal semantics for most programming languages, which limits the ability to prove program correctness at scale. The experiment used an extended version of the WHILE language and involved writing semantics rules and proving their correctness in the Lean proof assistant. The process refined the semantics and handled complex aspects like memory reasoning. Basis AI's goal is to develop scalable verification methods to secure critical infrastructure software against increasingly capable AI-driven attacks by ensuring software correctness through formal proofs rather than relying solely on testing or informal specifications.

item.title: Mass General Brigham develops AI tool that predicts cancer survival from a single patient selfie using facial analysis and biological age estimation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers at Mass General Brigham have created an AI system that predicts cancer patient survival outcomes from a single facial photograph by estimating biological age and directly assessing survival risk. The tool, trained on over 40 million images, uses two models-FAHR-FaceAge and FAHR-FaceSurvival-that analyze different facial regions to provide complementary health insights. The study, published in Lancet Digital Health, found that patients who appeared biologically older had a higher risk of death during follow-up, while those who looked younger had a lower risk. The AI's predictions were consistent across various photo conditions and even after some plastic surgeries. Researchers suggest this technology could support personalized treatment decisions by providing a scalable, non-invasive method to assess patient health, though further validation is needed before widespread clinical use.

item.title: Privacy Layer project launches to enhance data privacy for frontier AI models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A new project called Privacy Layer has been introduced to improve privacy protections in advanced machine learning systems. It aims to safeguard user data while enabling the use of cutting-edge AI models. The project is available at privai-sandy.vercel.app and was recently discussed on Hacker News.

item.title: U.S. prosecutors say OpenAI employee accused of bugging office had ties to Saudi royal family
item.description: U.S. prosecutors allege that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi Arabian national and former OpenAI employee arrested on October 9, had connections to the Saudi royal family while accused of bugging OpenAI's office. The FBI detained Alfozan following the discovery of surveillance devices at OpenAI's premises. This case highlights concerns about insider threats and foreign influence within major AI companies.

item.title: Amazon launches TorchNeuron tool to run PyTorch AI apps on its Trainium chip, aiming to reduce Nvidia's dominance in AI hardware [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Amazon Web Services introduced TorchNeuron, a tool that enables AI developers to run PyTorch applications on Amazon's Trainium chip with minimal code changes. This move targets Nvidia's entrenched position in AI hardware by making it easier for startups to use Amazon's AI chip and cloud infrastructure. TorchNeuron integrates with PyTorch, which is used by about 85% of AI apps, and allows developers to switch to Trainium by changing just one configuration line. Amazon is also contributing code to PyTorch to reduce its Nvidia-specific dependencies, aiming to make the framework more hardware-agnostic and expand developer choice beyond Nvidia GPUs. AWS argues that using Trainium offers cost and performance benefits by supporting both AI training and inference on a single platform tightly integrated with its cloud services. This strategy could challenge Nvidia's software advantage and reshape the AI hardware ecosystem if widely adopted.

item.title: The Information names new reporters for OpenAI, Google, Asia AI and data centers, and tech capital markets coverage [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The Information has appointed new reporters to cover key beats including OpenAI, Google, Asia-focused AI and data centers, and tech capital markets. Jemima McEvoy will cover OpenAI, Ryan Barwick joins to report on Google, Claudia Chong will focus on AI and data centers in Asia from Singapore, and Alex Eichenstein will cover tech capital markets and finance. Jemima McEvoy previously wrote for The Information's Weekend section and has reported on notable figures and companies in tech and venture capital. Ryan Barwick comes from Axios with experience covering advertising technology and consumer deals. Claudia Chong has a background in risk advisory and investigative journalism in Southeast Asia, while Alex Eichenstein has covered healthcare deals and private equity shifts at The Deal. These hires aim to strengthen The Information's reporting on rapidly evolving technology sectors and markets, reflecting the publication's commitment to exclusive and in-depth business journalism.

item.title: OpenCode reports breach of older system exposing API keys, leading to unauthorized AI usage charges for 1.4% of users [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenCode, an open source AI coding agent, disclosed a security breach affecting 1.4% of users on its OpenCode Console platform, where attackers accessed stored API keys and caused unauthorized charges on users' AI accounts. The company notified affected users and is working with AI providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google to block compromised keys and issue refunds. The breach highlighted challenges in defending against AI-driven cyberattacks, as some AI models used for defense refused to analyze malicious code due to safety filters. OpenCode gained access to OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program, which offers less restrictive AI models, improving their investigation capabilities. The incident remains ongoing amid a broader rise in AI-enabled cyber threats globally.

item.title: The Washington Post reports on leaked Anthropic bill revealing AI development costs and sparking transparency debates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The Washington Post published a report on a leaked bill from Anthropic, an artificial intelligence company, which details the company's financial and operational expenses related to AI development. This disclosure has prompted discussions about transparency and the economic aspects of AI research. The leaked document provides insight into Anthropic's internal cost structures and spending, shedding light on the financial challenges faced by AI firms. The report has drawn attention to the broader implications for how AI companies manage and disclose their expenditures in a rapidly evolving industry.

item.title: Tolan raises $30 million for its AI companion app with over 250,000 active users, doubling its total funding and pushing valuation above $268 million [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Tolan, an AI companion app designed to assist users with daily life management, relationships, and goal achievement, has secured an additional $30 million in funding from investors including Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew. This latest round doubles the startup's total capital raised and increases its estimated valuation to over $268 million. The app features a cartoonish character that supports users through tasks and emotional challenges, generating revenue through tiered memberships with annual recurring revenue in the double-digit millions. The app has attracted more than 250,000 active users who have engaged in over 70 million conversations in the past year, with a user base predominantly composed of women and parents. Tolan is noted for balancing helpfulness without being perceived as off-putting, distinguishing itself from other AI companions that have faced criticism or financial difficulties. However, the company faces potential competition from newer AI agents offering task planning and organization features, as well as legal risks associated with AI-powered emotional support.

item.title: Replika founder Eugenia Kuyda launches Wabi, a multiplayer personal AI assistant evolving her 12-year-old chatbot vision [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Eugenia Kuyda, founder of Replika, has launched Wabi, a personal AI assistant app that builds on her original chatbot concept presented 12 years ago at TechCrunch Disrupt. Wabi allows users to manage multiple AI threads for different tasks and goals, with custom apps and shared group chat features. Wabi 2.0 automatically creates relevant apps and threads based on user data like email, aiming to reduce the need for manual setup. Its multiplayer design enables shared AI interactions among users, differentiating it from single-thread assistants. The app is SOC 2 compliant and stores most data in the U.S., emphasizing privacy and security.

item.title: Tenstorrent raises $1.5 billion at $6.2 billion valuation to scale open-weight AI chips after rejecting acquisition offers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on AI inference, raised $1.5 billion in funding at a $6.2 billion valuation to expand its open-weight AI chip production. The company, led by CEO Jim Keller, decided to remain independent after acquisition interest from Intel and Qualcomm at valuations up to $5 billion earlier this year. The funding round was led by Trace Capital and Innovation X, with participation from Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price. Tenstorrent plans to use the capital to scale chips optimized for serving open-weight AI models and video generation, positioning itself among startups challenging Nvidia's dominance in AI hardware.

item.title: DeepSeek collaborates with Huawei to influence AI chip design for 2027 and beyond, aiming to reduce reliance on Nvidia technology [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: DeepSeek is working closely with Huawei Technologies to shape the design of future AI chips, aiming to help China develop advanced AI models without depending on Nvidia's technology. Huawei engineers have incorporated DeepSeek's input into design decisions related to data processing and model calculations for chips expected to launch next year and later. To facilitate this collaboration, Huawei engineers have been stationed at DeepSeek's offices for an extended period, indicating a deep integration of their efforts.

item.title: RuneScape Bench releases video exploring MMOs for AI agents
item.description: RuneScape Bench has published a video discussing the use of massively multiplayer online games (MMOs) as environments for AI agents. The video examines how MMOs can serve as complex, interactive platforms for training and testing agent behaviors in dynamic virtual worlds.

item.title: OpenAI improves GPT-6 models for coding and migrating low-resource programming languages like COBOL and Fortran with new MultiLangBench and COBOL migration evaluations [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: OpenAI has enhanced its GPT-6 models to better handle low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic, which are critical for infrastructure and essential services but have limited training data. The improvements focus on building new software and migrating existing code while preserving functionality, addressing challenges faced by developers maintaining legacy systems. The company developed two evaluations: MultiLangBench, which tests building a SQLite-compatible database engine across 20 languages, and a COBOL migration evaluation that assesses migrating COBOL programs to languages like C++, Java, and Python. GPT-6 Astra achieved an 87.4% average pass rate on MultiLangBench, up from 26.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol, and GPT-6.1 Sol reached up to 97.9% accuracy on COBOL migration tasks, significantly outperforming previous models while reducing costs. These advancements demonstrate substantial progress in AI-assisted software development for underrepresented programming languages, potentially aiding teams in maintaining and modernizing critical legacy systems more efficiently.

item.title: Anthropic proposes reducing reward hacking in AI by localizing bad behavior instead of penalizing it [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic's Alignment Science blog discusses a new approach to mitigating reward hacking in AI systems by focusing on localizing and addressing specific bad behaviors rather than applying broad penalties. This method aims to improve AI alignment by targeting problematic actions more precisely, potentially leading to safer and more reliable AI behavior.

item.title: US government detains former OpenAI engineer accused of spying with evidence of Saudi government ties and flight risk [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A former OpenAI engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, was detained by the US government on charges of spying after allegedly bugging a top-secret conference room to steal company secrets. The FBI found evidence including a folder labeled "Saudi Gov Docs" on his phone and communications with a Saudi royal family member, suggesting possible espionage for Saudi Arabia amid the country's AI initiatives. Alfozan, a Saudi national and US permanent resident, had booked a one-way ticket to Riyadh paid for by the Saudi government and was considered a flight risk. The US attorney highlighted his financial resources, Saudi bank accounts, and connections to Saudi officials as factors supporting continued detention. Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse agreed to keep Alfozan detained pending trial due to national security concerns and the risk of fleeing the country.

item.title: New York City Council questions SpaceX over sexualized image of its AI speaker Grok [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The New York City Council questioned SpaceX about a sexualized image of its AI speaker, Grok, which the company had produced. The image raised concerns about the appropriateness and representation of the technology. SpaceX faced scrutiny over the depiction and its implications.

item.title: CoreWeave's bonds enter distressed territory amid concerns over AI industry debt and private credit bubble risks [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: CoreWeave's bonds have slipped into distressed territory, with investors demanding yields 1,000 basis points above government bonds, raising concerns about the company's heavy debt load and its impact on the broader AI industry. The company's shares have dropped over 20% since the distress was noted, and worries about a private credit bubble in AI infrastructure financing have surfaced, especially after cofounder Brannin McBee expressed intentions to secure investment-grade debt to tap into insurer capital. CoreWeave owes more than $35 billion, largely due to pioneering GPU-backed loans, but it operates a business that currently loses money by selling compute services. Despite this, the company holds $103.7 billion in remaining customer obligations, including contracts with Microsoft, OpenAI, and likely Nvidia, which provide some revenue stability. However, investor anxiety around CoreWeave's debt has also affected other AI-related companies like Oracle, indicating broader market concerns about the sustainability of debt-fueled AI infrastructure growth.

item.title: Federal judge orders former OpenAI engineer accused of spying to remain in custody amid concerns over Saudi government support [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A federal judge ruled that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a covert listening device in a company conference room, must remain in custody while awaiting trial due to concerns about his ties to Saudi Arabia and the risk of flight. Prosecutors highlighted the Saudi government's offer to support Alfozan's bail without conditions, which the judge described as a "blank check." Alfozan, who had frequent communications with a member of the Saudi royal family and was allegedly recruited for a Saudi AI initiative, was fired by OpenAI after the discovery of the device and subsequently arrested. Authorities found additional recording components at his home and evidence suggesting attempts to monitor other OpenAI locations. His defense denies any covert spying activities, attributing the electronics to personal projects. item.title: Why Upstart Banks May Have to Keep Raising Money
item.description: The Trump administration has opened the door for entrepreneurs to start new banks in the U.S., many funded by venture capital. But there's a catch for fast-growing newcomers. Upstarts like Palmer Luckey's Erebor Bank, as well as other new entrants like Openreserve and Augustus, will likely have to keep raising money as they grow to maintain the capital cushion they need to satisfy bank regulatory requirements. That's a contrast to most startups, which use fresh venture money to pay for operating expenses and expand the business. Regulators require banks to maintain a capital cushion to absorb potential losses and protect depositors. That cushion is typically measured through a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio, which measures a bank's capital relative to assets including cash, loans and investments. For instance, a bank subject to a 12% minimum tier 1 leverage ratio needs to maintain at least $12 in capital for every $100 in assets. As a bank attracts more deposits, its assets, such as loans, typically grow too, increasing the amount of capital it needs to meet that minimum ratio. Established banks can build up their capital through their profits, but newer banks that aren't yet profitable have to rely instead on raising fresh equity from investors. Startup banks have already been raising significant funding to get their businesses off the ground or as deposits grow. Erebor Bank is set to raise $1.5 billion in a fresh fundraising round at an $8 billion valuation before the investment, after launching with $625 million in committed capital in February. The fundraising comes as the bank has seen its deposits surge to $7 billion as of the end of September, up from $4 billion at the end of the prior quarter. Meanwhile, Openreserve, an a16z crypto-backed bank that raised $25 million in September, said it expects to announce an additional capital raise to meet its regulatory requirements ahead of its planned opening early next year. Then there's Augustus, a startup bank focused on serving fintech companies. It raised $180 million in a Tiger Global Management-led round in July at a $1 billion valuation and expects to open later this year. Regulators give capital ratios to each bank based on their assessment of the institution's business plans and risks. Newly created banks typically face tougher capital requirements than established banks. For the first three years of operation, Erebor and Openreserve must each maintain a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio of 12%, while Augustus faces a 10% minimum. Established banks, by comparison, typically have ratios of between 5% and 6%. "There's no question that the regulators treat de novo banks-new banks-differently than they do well-established banks," according to Brian Graham, a partner and co-founder at consulting firm Klaros Group who advises clients on bank charter applications. Graham noted that the extra capital requirements typically go away after a bank has been operating for three years. The upstart banks are generally pursuing relatively new business models or focusing on sectors big banks typically avoid. Erebor Bank, for example, has gained traction in areas prioritized by the Trump administration, such as defense startups and crypto firms, and is expanding in geographies traditional banks typically avoid, including Venezuela and Syria. In addition to making minimum capital requirements, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.-a banking regulator-imposed an unusual condition on its approval of Erebor for the deposit insurance program. Under a capital-call provision, Erebor's investors must contribute additional capital if the bank doesn't meet its minimum capital requirements, according to a filing. The filing didn't disclose which investors are required to provide the capital backstop. In the meantime, upstart banks that are looking to drive revenue growth from lending rather than fees will likely need to tap investors to build their capital. "To the extent the bank's business model is reliant materially on the balance sheet for revenue and net income, you're going to need to raise more capital to drive growth," Klaros' Graham said. Openreserve, for its part, plans to make loans backed by traditional assets and turn them into digital tokens that can trade on blockchain, potentially providing a new source of loans for investors and lenders in the crypto market. For example, it plans to lend businesses money against their trade receivables, turning those assets into digital tokens to make them easier to trade. "Our ambition is to be the on-chain GSIB," referring to a globally systemically important bank, said Dee Choubey, founder and CEO of Openreserve. The bank also plans to issue its own stablecoin and to offer tokenized deposits, digital versions of traditional bank accounts that earn interest. Over time, it aims to provide banking and payment services to other digital banks. Augustus plans to focus on helping fintech, crypto and remittance companies move money across borders using both traditional banking systems and stablecoins. That will put it in competition with existing banks like United Texas Bank, which has become dominant in processing dollar payments for overseas crypto exchanges. "Whenever someone outside the U.S. touches the dollar through a local bank or local fintech, that always has to be facilitated by a U.S. nationally chartered clearing bank, so we provide that service," said Augustus CEO Ferdinand Dabitz. In Europe, the bank already counts crypto exchange Kraken among its clients. Augustus is less focused on activities like lending, however, and has a lower ratio than the other two. The company has raised significantly more than its initial capital requirement, which could lessen the need for more fundraising in the near term. "We are less focused on the credit side as other market participants. We think the clearing side is really where we shine," Dabitz said. item.title: Your Office Isn't Spy Proof [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Welcome, Weekenders! A song has been stuck on loop in my mind for days now. Yeah, this one. C'mon, haven't you heard the big, brassy James Bond theme playing too? We have an honest-to-goodness spy scandal on our hands! That would be the affair over at OpenAI, where the FBI has arrested a former engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, for allegedly placing a toilet paper-wrapped recording device in a conference room. Why'd he do it? The Justice Department wasn't explicit in its press release announcing Alfozan's arrest, though the statement does make sure to prominently describe him as a "national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia," implying, obviously, that he was hoping to spy on OpenAI for the Saudis. I expect a not unsizable part of Silicon Valley experienced some schadenfreude when reading about the turn of events at OpenAI. I'd advise against indulging in that feeling, because when I struck up conversations with a few corporate security consultants and surveillance experts over the last few days, they all echoed the same sentiment: Plenty of companies risk ending up in the same situation-especially as they move quickly in today's era of frenzied, heightened competition. A discomforting thought, eh? "Organizations can sometimes be moving so fast that they often don't understand that there's an issue associated with somebody until that person's on board and up to no good," said Bill Priestap, a former head of FBI counterintelligence who now runs his own security consultancy, Trenchcoat Advisors. "Meaning they're recruiting, and they're under such pressure to get the right people and get them on board that in many regards, they end up with a minimal understanding of the people they're bringing on board." Well, good thing there hasn't been an enormous, frantic hiring binge lately. Ha ha ha. If you're starting to feel a little paranoid, I strongly, strongly advise against talking to someone like David Abbott, a San Francisco private detective, to find out how easy it is to bug an office. Such conversations will only further unnerve you-you might end up holding your next board meeting in your home basement, Tony Soprano style-because according to Abbott, it's pretty darn easy to install a recording device. A suitable one can be bought for less than $100. Some of the popular ones resemble phone chargers, which get tucked into a power socket, hidden in plain sight. He's also seen surveillance devices in fake coffee cups-you know, like the ones that might lie casually around an office-and quite a few in fake smoke alarms. More bad news: Should you find such a device, it's like spotting an ant in your kitchen. One ant suggests the presence of more ants. "If I'm doing a bug sweep, just because I find one does not mean there isn't a second," said Abbott. "If you find one, there's going to be two. If you find two, there's going to be three. You just keep looking." What happened at OpenAI underscores Abbott's warning. There, Alfozan, the alleged spy, did plant two bugs. Well, he tried to do so. Alfozan, not the sort who seems like he would've ever earned double 0 status, had placed another bug in a bag that he then mislaid: He reported it missing and had to go pick it up from the company's lost and found. OK, if I've spooked the heck out of you, I guess I can offer some solace by pointing you in the direction of Eric and Greg Levesque, whose Salt Lake City-based startup, Strider Technologies, has raised $110 million in the last few years to sell AI-powered software to businesses that monitors email and other internal communications, flagging suspicious behavior and possible espionage attempts. (Yes, the company's name is a reference to Strider from "The Lord of the Rings," the nom de cloak of Aragorn, the character Viggo Mortensen plays.) "What we've found is that companies are not always dealing with trained intelligence operatives. Like, they're dealing with scientists or legitimate engineers who have been approached or coerced in some form or fashion and are now working on behalf of someone else," said Greg Levesque. "They can leave a lot of digital exhaust."-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) The Information's Must-Read Stories Cursor Staff Investigated Whether Confidential Data Reached SpaceX for AI Training Anthropic's Rapid but Slowing Growth Could Weigh on IPO Valuation Andreessen Horowitz, General Catalyst Race to Secure the Chips Their Startups Need How Microsoft's New Office Chief Fixed Copilot and Won Over Nadella Listening: "Reaching Out" As the pandemic shut down the world in 2020, Sayre Quevedo, then a producer for The New York Times' "The Daily" podcast, quit his job and headed out to Los Angeles, hoping for a chance at self-reinvention. To cope with those tumultuous times, he decided to pursue a documentary project, recording every phone call. Had nothing else of import happened in his life, Quevedo might've wound up with an intriguing time capsule. But something quite unusual did occur: Just months after moving to LA, he and his twin brother, Connor, happened to finally locate their biological father, whom they'd never before met. He worked as a barber-blocks from where Sayre lived. "Reaching Out," a new podcast co-produced by NPR station KCRW that won a top prize in the Tribeca Festival's expanded podcast categories, is a starkly intimate account of their journey to meet him and their reconciliation with each other, their lives and what life might've been like if their father hadn't been a total stranger who happened to be just down the street.-Abram Brown Reading: "Sitcom" by Chuck Lorre and "Emperor of Nothing" by Blake J. Harris Chuck Lorre, the indefatigable TV showrunner, writer and producer, has kept the masses laughing for years-and years-and years, with a list of hits that includes "Two and a Half Men," "The Big Bang Theory" and "Dharma and Greg." Those are sitcoms, a term Lorre acknowledges once made him practically break out in hives, since it was often used to cheapen what he sees as grueling, high-touch art. With spicy good humor, he reclaims the word in his new memoir about his time in Hollywood, "Sitcom." "The truth is, making a live studio audience laugh for twenty-odd minutes every week, for twenty-two weeks, is incredibly hard and unbelievably stressful," Lorre writes. "If you're one of those people who insist on labeling all sitcoms as being cheap, juvenile and unsophisticated, well...all I can say is, blow me." I'd say "Sitcom" functions as a good primer on managing talent, too, and Lorre attests to having learned the importance of keeping out of the way. "Creativity needs air to breathe," he writes. To do the opposite risks turning a leader into "one of those plastic bags you get at the dry cleaners that can kill small children." Lorre also takes the opportunity to set down what he sees as good comedy's basic tenets and decry the medium's basest impulse: to write only about stupid people doing stupid things: "A better, perhaps deeper means to achieving laughter involves pain and suffering." Such a sentiment is most certainly shared by Larry David of "Seinfeld" and "Curb Your Enthusiasm," the subject of "Emperor of Nothing," a biography that won his reluctant cooperation. (When author Blake J. Harris finally wore David down, Harris received a two-line email from him: "Oh Jesus. If we must.") As with "Sitcom," "Emperor of Nothing" charts a remarkable rise across Hollywood from an inauspicious start: Lorre was a wannabe musician before his TV run, while David was a little-known stand-up comic with an unremarkable series of TV writing jobs before co-creating "Seinfeld." Like Lorre, David describes the process of penning comedy as an arduous affair. And by David's own telling, the process of sitting down to write a new "Seinfeld" season would bring on full panic. "That always seemed like a daunting prospect," he recalled. "Especially because all the good ideas were used up the year before." Fortunately, David had his friendship with the show's eponymous star, Jerry Seinfeld, one of many people within David's orbit who gave interviews for "Emperor of Nothing." "I would always say, 'All we have to do is write today,'" Seinfeld said. Or as David recalled: "Jerry always talked me off the ledge."-A.B. Watching: "War" No one does a charming, self-involved cad better than Dominic West, the British character actor who first washed ashore in America as "The Wire"'s Detective McNulty and then again in Showtime's "The Affair" and in the final two seasons of "The Crown" as Prince Charles. In "War," HBO's new high-tension legal drama, he's tech billionaire Morgan Henderson, a fellow championing a safer, more responsible social media-while embroiled in an increasingly messy divorce from his Hollywood star wife, Carla (Sienna Miller). Much of that mess is Morgan's own doing: He looks wonderful in his Savile Row trousers-he just has trouble keeping them on. As Morgan and Carla gird for an extended battle, they assemble a posse of cutthroat attorneys, who find their impulsive clients constantly upending their carefully laid strategies. That flock of legal eagles includes a handsome rogue, Johnny (Archie Renaux), a lad from working-class south London who sees a chance to ascend by, uh, redefining zealous representation. Backstabbing and double crosses abound.-A.B.
